label: rem:discrete-chain
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:discrete-chain}
The continuous-time chain with generator $-{\mathscr{L}}$ can be simulated by a
simple discrete-time chain. Let $B\ge\max_{S\in\Omega,\,u\in{\mathcal{U}}}|r_u(S)|$
be any known bound on the rates. From the current state $S\in\Omega$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),nosep,leftmargin=2em]
 \item With probability $1/2$, stay at $S$.
 \item Otherwise, choose $u\in{\mathcal{U}}$ uniformly at random, and
 \begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=1.5em]
  \item if $u\notin S$ and $S+u\in\Omega$, move to $S+u$ with probability
  $\mu(S+u)/(B\mu(S))$;
  \item if $u\in S$ {and $S-u\in\Omega$}, move to $S-u$ with probability $\nu(S-u)/(B\nu(S))$;
  \item otherwise, stay at $S$.
 \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}
Each probability in (2) is at most $1$ by the choice of $B$. The
resulting transition matrix is $P=I-{\mathscr{L}}/(2nB)$, which is lazy and
reversible with respect to $\rho$, and its spectral gap is that of ${\mathscr{L}}$
divided by $2nB$. The Poincar\'e inequality below therefore gives the
mixing bound \cref{eq:poincare-mixing} with $R=nB$.

body_md:
\label{rmk:curvature-LC-generalization}
                                                                            
\Cref{thm:curvature-convolution} can be viewed as a generalization of
\cref{thm:log-concave-convolution}. For log-concave measures, translating
$g_\mu(\bm{x}),g_\nu(\bm{x})$ to
$g_\mu(\mathbf1+\bm{x}),g_\nu(\mathbf1+\bm{x})$ gives downward-closed measures
with zero curvature by \cref{prop:flc-curvature}.
After reducing to homogeneous polynomials whose degrees sum to $n$
(see \cref{app:convolution-proofs}), these translations preserve the
coefficient of $\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$. The translated weights, i.e. the coefficients of $g_{\mu}(\mathbf{1} + \bm{x}), g_{\nu}(\mathbf{1} + \bm{x})$, are respectively
\[
 \widehat\mu(S)=\sum_{T\supseteq S}\mu(T),
 \qquad \widehat\nu(S)=\sum_{T\supseteq S}\nu(T).
\]
These sums each admit an $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ since $\mu,\nu$ are log-concave~\cite{AnariEtAl2019}.
Using sufficiently accurate estimates of the queried weights and
controlling the accumulated sampling error gives the reduction,
with additional polynomial overhead. We state
\cref{thm:log-concave-convolution} separately to give a direct
algorithm using the original evaluation oracles and a sharper
running-time bound.

label: rmk:gurvits-capacity
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:gurvits-capacity}
For a nonzero finitely supported measure $w$ on $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n$,
write $g_w(\bm x)=\sum_{\bm k}w(\bm k)\bm x^{\bm k}$.
Its \emph{Gurvits capacity} at $\bm\alpha\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}^n$ is
\[
 \operatorname{Cap}_{\bm\alpha}(g_w)\coloneqq
 \inf_{\bm x\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^n}\frac{g_w(\bm x)}{\bm x^{\bm\alpha}}.
\]
The Gurvits capacity at $\bm \alpha \in \operatorname{supp} w$ is always an upper bound on $w(\bm \alpha)$.
To see this, define the distribution
$p_{\bm z}(\bm k)=w(\bm k)\bm z^{\bm k}/g_w(\bm z)$.
If $\bm\alpha\in\operatorname{supp} w$, then
\[
 \operatorname{Cap}_{\bm\alpha}(g_w)
 =\frac{w(\bm\alpha)}{\sup_{\bm z>0}p_{\bm z}(\bm\alpha)} \geq w(\bm \alpha).
\]
                                                                        
                                                                     
                 
Intuitively, it gives the best possible approximation of $w(\bm \alpha)$ that we can get by only tuning external fields applied to the base measure.

After taking logarithms, the optimization over external fields above has
a dual formulation as a minimum $\operatorname{KL}$-divergence convex program with prescribed mean,
or equivalently, a weighted maximum-entropy convex program~\cite{SinghVishnoi2014Entropy}.
For $\bm\alpha\in\operatorname{supp} w$, let
\[
 q^*=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{q:\,\mathbb E_q[\bm X]=\bm\alpha}
 D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q\,\middle\|\,p_{\mathbf{1}}\right),
\]
where $q$ ranges over probability distributions on $\operatorname{supp} w$,
$p_{\mathbf{1}}=w/g_w(\mathbf1)$ is the normalized measure, and
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ denotes Kullback--Leibler divergence.
Entropy duality and the KL Pythagorean identity~\cite[Theorem~3.2]{CsiszarShields2004}
give
\[
 \log\frac{\operatorname{Cap}_{\bm\alpha}(g_w)}{w(\bm\alpha)}
 =D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\delta_{\bm\alpha}\,\middle\|\,q^*\right)
 =-\log q^*(\bm\alpha),
\]
where $\delta_{\bm\alpha}$ is the point mass at $\bm\alpha$.
In other words, we adjust the original distribution as little as possible
in KL divergence to obtain mean $\bm\alpha$. The approximation ratio is
the reciprocal of the probability that this distribution assigns to
$\bm\alpha$ itself.

For every homogeneous \emph{real stable} polynomial $g$ of degree $n$ in $n$
variables with nonnegative coefficients,
\[
 \frac{n!}{n^n}\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf1}(g)
 \le [x_1\cdots x_n]g
 \le \operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf1}(g).
\]
The upper bound follows from the definition of capacity.
Gurvits~\cite{Gurvits2006} proves the lower bound, showing that capacity
overestimates the coefficient by at most a factor $n^n/n!$.
For the permanent of a nonnegative matrix $A$, he uses the polynomial
$g(\bm{x})=\prod_{i=1}^n(\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j)$;
for mixed discriminants, he uses
$g(\bm{x})=\det(\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i)$, where the $A_i$ are positive semidefinite.
This approach has since been extended to other settings; see
\cref{subsec:prior-work}.

In our setting, the target coefficient
$[\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]Z_{t,\bm{x}}=Z_\cap$ is independent of $t$.
For fixed $t$, the Gurvits capacity is
\[
 \operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf1}(Z_{t,\bm{x}})=
 \inf_{\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\frac{Z_{t,\bm{x}}}{\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}
 =\exp\left(\inf_{\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\Phi(\bm{y})\right).
\]
When $Z_\cap>0$, the probability interpretation above gives the
approximation ratio
\[
 \frac{\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf1}(Z_{t,\bm x})}{Z_\cap}
 =\frac{1}{\sup_{\bm z>0}\pi_{t,\bm z}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)}.
\]
Under the hypotheses of \cref{lem:field-concavity}, this ratio satisfies
\[
 1\le\frac{\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf1}(Z_{t,\bm{x}})}{Z_\cap}
 \le\left(1-\frac{4n\sqrt t}{\gamma}\right)^{-1},
 \qquad 4n\sqrt t<\gamma.
\]
Indeed, $\Phi$ is bounded below and has a globally bounded Hessian,
so it admits points $\bm{y}$ with arbitrarily small gradient; applying
\cref{lem:field-concavity} to the corresponding fields $\bm{z}=\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}$
gives the upper bound on the ratio.
Thus decreasing $t$ makes the capacity bound nearly tight.

The permanent algorithm of Jerrum--Sinclair--Vigoda~\cite{JerrumSinclairVigoda2004}

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the chain is reversible, ${\mathcal{L}}$ is self-adjoint and positive
semidefinite with respect to $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\pi$; since it
is irreducible, its kernel consists of the constant functions. Hence
${\mathcal{L}}$ is positive definite on $\mathbf1^\perp$
{(the functions with mean zero under $\pi$)}, and ${\mathcal{L}}^{1/2}$ is a
bijection of $\mathbf1^\perp$. Both ratios are unchanged when a constant
is added to $f$, so we may take $f\in\mathbf1^\perp\setminus\{0\}$, for
which $ \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[f\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi}\left[f\right]} =\langle f,f\rangle_\pi$. Substituting
$g\coloneqq{\mathcal{L}}^{1/2}f$ gives
\begin{align*}
 \frac{\langle{\mathcal{L}} f,{\mathcal{L}} f\rangle_\pi}{\langle f,{\mathcal{L}} f\rangle_\pi}
 &=\frac{\langle g,{\mathcal{L}} g\rangle_\pi}{\langle g,g\rangle_\pi},
\end{align*}
and $g$ ranges over $\mathbf1^\perp\setminus\{0\}$ as $f$ does. Hence
the two infima coincide.

label: lem:sampling-to-counting
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sampling-to-counting}
Let $m\ge1$, let $w:\{0,1\}^m\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}$ be nonzero, and write
$Z\coloneqq\sum_{\sigma}w(\sigma)$ and $\pi(\sigma)\coloneqq w(\sigma)/Z$.
For every nonempty conditional law obtained by fixing coordinates,
suppose a sampler, given any starting state in its support and an
accuracy $0<\tau<1$, returns
a sample in that support whose distribution is within total variation distance $\tau$ of
the conditional law, using fresh independent randomness.
Given an evaluation oracle for $w$, a state $\sigma_0\in\operatorname{supp} w$, and
$0<\varepsilon,\delta<1$, one can compute $\widehat Z$ satisfying
\[
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbf{Pr}\left[(1-\varepsilon)Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z\right]}
  {\mathbf{Pr}_{}\left[(1-\varepsilon)Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z\right]} \ge1-\delta.
\]
On every execution, the algorithm uses
$Q=O(m^3\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2m/\delta))$ sampler calls, each with total variation distance at most
$\tau=\varepsilon/(16m)$, one evaluation of $w$, and $O(Q)$ additional
arithmetic operations. It supplies a starting state for every call.

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{lem:field-concavity}, it suffices to find $\bm{y}$ with
$\|\nabla\Phi(\bm{y})\|_\infty\le\eta\coloneqq 1/(4n)$ and return $\bm{z}\coloneqq \exp(\bm{y})$:
then $n(\eta+ 4\sqrt t)=1/2$. We apply
\cref{thm:stochastic-coordinate-descent} with
$d=n$, $L=\sigma=1$, $H_0=B$, and $\bm{x}_0=\bm{0}$.
For $(S,T)\sim\pi_{t,\exp(\bm{y})}$, the vector
$\bm{G}\coloneqq \mathbf1_S+\mathbf1_T-\mathbf1$ satisfies
\begin{align*}
 \nabla\Phi(\bm{y})&= \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[\bm{G}\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[\bm{G}\right]} ,&
 \nabla^2\Phi(\bm{y})&=\operatorname{Cov}(\bm{G})\succeq0,\\
 \partial_u^2\Phi(\bm{y})&= \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[G_u\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{}\left[G_u\right]} \le1,&
 \bm{G}&\in[-1,1]^n.
\end{align*}
Thus $\Phi$ is convex and coordinatewise $1$-smooth, and Hoeffding's
lemma gives coordinatewise $1$-sub-Gaussian oracle noise.
When $Z_\cap>0$, every complementary pair contributes its unchanged
weight to $\exp(\Phi(\bm{y}))$. Writing
$M\coloneqq \max_S\mu(S)\max_T\nu(T)$, we therefore have
\begin{align*}
 \Phi(\bm{y})&\ge\log Z_\cap\ge\log\frac{M}{{\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu},&
 \Phi(\bm{0})&\le\log(4^nM).
\end{align*}
Thus the required gap bound is at most $B$, so take $H_0\coloneqq B$;
no minimizing point need exist.

Take $\delta=1/64$ in \cref{thm:stochastic-coordinate-descent}.
The algorithm uses at most $Q_{\mathrm{cd}}=O(n^4B\log(2B))$ gradient
samples and $O(T'Q_{\mathrm{cd}})$ operations, where $T'$ bounds the
cost of one gradient sample. It also gives
$\|\bm{y}\|_1=O(B/\eta+\eta)=O(nB)$ for every queried or returned point,
which proves \cref{eq:balancing-bounds}.
We stop and report failure before exceeding any of these bounds.
Thus they also hold when $Z_\cap=0$; when $Z_\cap>0$, this stopping
rule does not change the algorithm with exact samples.

Supply each gradient sample using \cref{cor:bases-pair-sampling},
with fresh randomness and total variation error at most
$1/(64Q_{\mathrm{cd}})$.
By \cref{rem:approximate-sampling}, these sampling errors add at most
$1/64$ to the failure probability. Hence the algorithm finds the
required field with probability at least $1-1/64-1/64=31/32$
when $Z_\cap>0$.

For the running time, the field bound gives
$n\log(z_{\max}/z_{\min})=O(n^2B)$ at every query.
Since $t^{-1}=256 n^2$ and $B=\Theta(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu))$,
\cref{cor:bases-pair-sampling} gives $T'=O(n^6B)$ operations and
value-oracle calls per gradient sample.
Multiplying by $Q_{\mathrm{cd}}$ proves the claimed bound;
the $O(nQ_{\mathrm{cd}})$ additional operations cost less.
The field updates can be implemented using arithmetic operations only;
see \cref{app:counting-arithmetic}.

label: eq:counting-factorization
title: Proof
body_md:
The cases $a=0$ or $b=0$ are evaluated directly, so assume $n\ge2$.
We choose fields making complementary pairs frequent, then estimate
the two unknown factors in
\begin{align}\label{eq:counting-factorization}
 Z_\cap&=\frac{Z_{t,\bm{z}}}{\bm{z}^{{\mathcal{U}}}} \times
          \pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S).
\end{align}
Let $B,t$ be as in \cref{cor:balanced-fields}, and put
$\beta\coloneqq \varepsilon/4$ and $\delta_0\coloneqq 1/64$.
Apply \cref{cor:balanced-fields}; if it reports failure, return zero.
Otherwise fix the returned field $\bm{z}$. When $Z_\cap>0$, with probability
at least $1-2\delta_0$, this field satisfies
$\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)\ge1/2$.

\paragraph{Estimating the normalizer.}
For any returned field $\bm{z}$, we apply
\cref{lem:sampling-to-counting} to the $2n$ membership bits of $(S,T)$,
with weight
\begin{align*}
 W(S,T)&\coloneqq \mu(S)\nu(T)t^{|S\cap T|}\bm{z}^S\bm{z}^T.
\end{align*}
The supplied pair $(S_0,T_0)$ is a valid starting state.

Each conditional law is obtained by restricting $\mu,\nu$ to the
prescribed inclusions and exclusions, with the same $t,\bm{z}$.
We keep the original ground set and the forced elements in each set,
so the degrees remain $a,b$. Inclusion replaces a generating polynomial
by its coordinate derivative times that variable; exclusion sets the
variable to zero. These operations preserve log-concavity, and the
coefficient ranges do not increase. For every nonempty
conditional law, both measures are nonzero. Thus \cref{cor:bases-pair-sampling} applies
to every conditional law.

\Cref{lem:sampling-to-counting}, with relative error
$\beta$ and failure probability $\delta_0$, therefore gives an estimate
$\widehat Z$ of $Z_{t,\bm{z}}$ using
$O(n^3\beta^{-2}\log(2n/\delta_0))$ conditional samples, each within
total variation distance $\beta/(32n)$ of its law.
The sample counts and running times are bounded on every execution.

\paragraph{Combining the estimates.}
Independently draw
$m=\lceil8\beta^{-2}\log(2/\delta_0)\rceil$ pairs from $\pi_{t,\bm{z}}$,
each to total variation error $\beta/4$, and let $\widehat p$ be the
fraction that are complementary. Conditional on the returned fields,
Hoeffding's inequality gives
$|\widehat p-\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)|\le\beta/2$ except with probability $\delta_0$:
the sampling bias is at most $\beta/4$, as is the fluctuation of
the empirical average. Return
\begin{align*}
 \widehat Z_\cap&\coloneqq \widehat p\,\widehat Z/\bm{z}^{{\mathcal{U}}}.
\end{align*}
{When the returned field satisfies
$\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)\ge1/2$ and both preceding
estimation bounds hold, this is a product of two estimates, each with
relative error at most $\beta$. These conditions hold jointly with
probability at least $1-4\delta_0>3/4$, so}
\begin{align*}
 (1-\beta)^2&\le\widehat Z_\cap/Z_\cap\le(1+\beta)^2,
\end{align*}
which implies relative error $\varepsilon$. If $Z_\cap=0$, every supported
pair fails the complementary-pair test. Thus every execution returns
zero, either at the field-finding step or because $\widehat p=0$.

\paragraph{Running time.}
Finding the field costs $O(n^{10}B^2\log(2B))$ by
\cref{cor:balanced-fields}. Throughout the self-reduction, the
coefficient ranges do not increase, and
$n\log(z_{\max}/z_{\min})=O(n^2B)$ by
\cref{eq:balancing-bounds}. Each restricted oracle uses one original
query and $O(n)$ operations to check the prescribed memberships.
Thus \cref{cor:bases-pair-sampling}, with $t^{-1}= 256 n^2$, bounds the
cost of a conditional sample by
\begin{align*}
 O\left(n^5\left(n^2B+\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)\right).
\end{align*}
Self-reduction uses $O(n^3\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2n))$ such samples.
Estimating the complementary-pair probability takes
$O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ additional samples and is covered by the same bound.
Since $B=\Theta(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu))$, the total cost is
\begin{align*}
 O\left(n^{10}B^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2\frac{2B}{\varepsilon}\right),
\end{align*}
as required by \cref{eq:main-cost}.

body_md:
By the reduction above, it suffices to estimate $Z_\cap$.
If $\max\{\kappa,\eta\}=0$, then $\eta=\kappa=0$ and
\cref{prop:zero-curvature-log-concavity} makes both generating polynomials
log-concave; the empty sets supply {starting sets of positive weight}. Thus
\cref{thm:log-concave-convolution} applies, and its cost is the first term in the stated bound.
It remains to treat the case $\max\{\eta,\kappa\}>0$, whose cost is the
second term.

\paragraph{The case $\max\{\eta,\kappa\}>0$.}
Interchange $\mu$ and $\nu$ if necessary so that $\nu$ has upward
spectral curvature $\kappa=\gamma>0$.
Since $\operatorname{supp}\nu$ is downward closed and hence connected, the final conclusion of \cref{lem:positive-curvature-support} gives
$\operatorname{supp}\nu=2^V$, where $V\coloneqq \{u:\nu(\{u\})>0\}$.
As in the reduction above, we may assume without loss of generality
that $V={\mathcal{U}}$, by pinning ${\mathcal{U}}\setminus V$ into $\mu$
and restricting to $V$ (returning zero if the pinning is infeasible,
and evaluating the case $V=\varnothing$ directly).
The measure $\mu$ still has downward-closed support,
and $\operatorname{supp}\nu=2^{{\mathcal{U}}}$.

To obtain a positive gap even when $\eta+\kappa=0$, decrease the field
of $\mu$ by setting
\begin{align*}
 t&\coloneqq 1-\frac{\varepsilon}{16n},&
 \widetilde\mu(A)&\coloneqq t^{|A|}\mu(A).
\end{align*}
This multiplies each ratio $\mu(S+u)/\mu(S)$ by $t$ and each ratio
$\mu(S+u+v)/\mu(S)$, for distinct $u,v\notin S$, by $t^2$.
Substituting into \cref{def:spectral-curvature} with parameter
$t\eta$ gives
\[
 A_S^{\widetilde\mu,t\eta}=t^2A_S^{\mu,\eta}\succeq0.
\]
Thus $\widetilde\mu$ has upward spectral curvature $t\eta$, and
\[
 \delta\coloneqq t\eta+\kappa
 =t(\eta+\kappa)+(1-t)\kappa
 \ge\frac{\varepsilon\gamma}{16n}.
\]
Let $\widetilde Z_\cap$ be the convolution value with $\mu$ replaced by
$\widetilde\mu$. Since $t^n\ge1-\varepsilon/16$,
\[
 (1-\varepsilon/16)Z_\cap\le t^n Z_\cap\le\widetilde Z_\cap\le Z_\cap.
\]
{Thus an estimate of $\widetilde Z_\cap$ with relative error
at most $\varepsilon/4$ also estimates $Z_\cap$ with \mbox{relative error at most $\varepsilon$}.}

Apply \cref{thm:poincare} with first factor $\widetilde\mu$ and second
factor $\nu^*(A)=\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus A)$, restricted to
$\Omega\coloneqq \operatorname{supp}\mu$. The second factor needs downward curvature
$\kappa$, which follows from
\[
 D_A^{\nu^*,\kappa}=A_{{\mathcal{U}}\setminus A}^{\nu,\kappa}\succeq0.
\]
Restricting $\nu^*$ to $\Omega$ leaves these matrices unchanged,
since every deletion of a set in $\Omega$ remains in $\Omega$.
The resulting chain samples
$\rho(A)\propto\widetilde\mu(A)\nu^*(A)$, has gap at least $\delta$,
and has rates
\begin{align*}
 q(A,A+u)&=t\frac{\mu(A+u)}{\mu(A)},&
 q(A,A-u)&=\frac{\nu(({\mathcal{U}}\setminus A)+u)}
                         {\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus A)}.
\end{align*}
Only the addition rates are multiplied by $t<1$.
Both rates are at most $B\coloneqq \chi\gamma$. Normalizing the rates by $2nB$
gives a lazy chain with gap at least
\[
 \frac{\delta}{2nB}
 \ge\frac{\varepsilon\gamma/(16n)}{2n\chi\gamma}
 =\frac{\varepsilon}{32\chi n^2}.
\]
The factor $\gamma$ cancels because the rate bound also contains $\gamma$.
The minimum stationary mass is at least $t^n/(2^n{\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)$,
and each step costs $O(1)$.
It starts from the supported empty set. The mixing bound
\cref{eq:poincare-mixing} gives a sample with total-variation
error $\tau$ in
\begin{align*}
 O\left(\frac{n^2\chi}{\varepsilon}
       \left[n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)+\log(1/\tau)\right]\right)
\end{align*}
steps. {The same bounds hold for the conditional distributions
obtained by fixing coordinates.}

\Cref{lem:sampling-to-counting}, applied to the $n$
membership bits with weight $\widetilde\mu(A)\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus A)$
and starting state $\varnothing$, estimates $\widetilde Z_\cap$ to
relative error $\varepsilon/4$, with success probability at least $3/4$, using
$O(n^3\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2n))$ conditional samples of accuracy
$\tau=\varepsilon/(64n)$. With fixed walk lengths, this gives total cost
\begin{align*}
 O\left(n^5\chi\varepsilon^{-3}\log(2n)
       \left[n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)+\log\frac{2n}{\varepsilon}\right]\right)
\end{align*}
arithmetic operations and value-oracle calls on every execution.
The tilt bound gives the required relative estimate of $Z_\cap$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $u\in V$. We show that $u$ can be added to every supported set
that does not already contain it. The key observation is that, along
an edge between two such sets, $u$ can be added at both endpoints or
at neither.

To see this, let $S,S+v\in\Omega$ with distinct $u,v\notin S$, and put
\[
 a=\frac{\omega(S+u)}{\omega(S)},\qquad
 b=\frac{\omega(S+v)}{\omega(S)}>0,\qquad
 c=\frac{\omega(S+u+v)}{\omega(S)}.
\]
The principal submatrix of $A_S^{\omega,\kappa}$ on $u,v$ is
\[
 M=\begin{pmatrix}a^2-\kappa a&ab-c\\ab-c&b^2-\kappa b\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
\]
If $a=0$, the first diagonal entry is zero, so positive semidefiniteness
forces the off-diagonal entry to vanish, giving $c=0$.
If $a>0$, positive semidefiniteness also gives
\[
 0\le (b,-a)M(b,-a)^{\mathsf T}
 =ab\bigl(2c-\kappa(a+b)\bigr),
\]
so $c\ge\kappa(a+b)/2>0$.
Thus $a>0$ if and only if $c>0$, proving the observation.

Now take any $S\in\Omega$ with $u\notin S$.
Since $u\in V$ and $\Omega$ is connected, there is a path in $\Omega$
from $S$ to a set containing $u$. Stop at the first such set.
The last step adds $u$, so $u$ can be added to the preceding set.
Every earlier edge has both endpoints omitting $u$; by the observation,
working backwards along the path shows that $u$ can also be added to $S$.
Since $u\in V$ was arbitrary, $\Omega$ is upward closed in $2^V$.

If $\Omega$ is also downward closed, then $\varnothing\in\Omega$.
Upward closure now gives $\Omega=2^V$, and {the description of $V$
as the set of elements $u$ with $\omega(\{u\})>0$ follows}.

Let $P\coloneqq \operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_A:A\in\operatorname{supp}\omega\}$, where
$\mathbf1_A$ is the incidence vector of $A$. This convex hull is the
\emph{Newton polytope} of $g_\omega$. Its vertices are precisely the
incidence vectors of sets in $\operatorname{supp}\omega$, and an \emph{edge} is a
one-dimensional face. By \cite[Proposition~10.4]{OveisGharan2020Lecture10},
every edge is parallel to a coordinate vector $\bm{e}_i$ or a difference
$\bm{e}_i-\bm{e}_j$. Consequently, a linear objective with no improving addition,
deletion, or exchange within $\operatorname{supp}\omega$ is globally optimal: these
moves include every incident edge. Starting at $A_0$, minimize
$|C\setminus A|+|A\cap O|$ by such moves. At most $n$ improvements,
each found with $O(n^2)$ queries, either produce a feasible set or
certify infeasibility. The convex hull of the feasible incidence vectors
is a face of $P$ and inherits its edge directions. Greedy additions and deletions
within this face therefore reach the maximum and minimum
cardinalities, visiting every intervening size in $O(n^2)$ further queries.

title: Proof
body_md:
We reduce counting proper two-colourings of a $3$-uniform hypergraph
to subset convolution. Deciding whether such a colouring exists is
$\mathsf{NP}$-complete~\cite{DinurRegevSmyth2005}.
Fix $\delta>0$ and a rational constant
$0<c<\min\{1,\delta/2\}$. For a $3$-uniform hypergraph
$\mathcal H=({\mathcal{U}},\mathcal F)$ with $n\coloneqq|{\mathcal{U}}|\ge1$, put
$a\coloneqq c/n$ and define
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal I&\coloneqq
 \{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}:F\nsubseteq S\text{ for every }F\in\mathcal F\},\\
 \mu(S)=\nu(S)&\coloneqq a^{|S|}\mathbf{1}[S\in\mathcal I].
\end{align*}
The two colour classes form a proper colouring exactly when both
belong to $\mathcal I$. Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 [\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]\bigl(g_\mu(\bm{x})g_\nu(\bm{x})\bigr)
 &=a^n\,\#\{\text{proper two-colourings of }\mathcal H\}.
\end{align*}
Since $a^n$ is known, it remains to verify the promised curvature and
oracle bounds.

Fix $S\in\mathcal I$, and let
$J_S\coloneqq\{u\in{\mathcal{U}}\setminus S:S+u\in\mathcal I\}$ be its
feasible additions. On $J_S$, define the symmetric matrix
\begin{align*}
 B_S(u,v)&\coloneqq
 \mathbf{1}[u\ne v,\ S+u+v\notin\mathcal I].
\end{align*}
Each row of $B_S$ has at most $n-1$ nonzero entries, all equal to one,
so $B_S\succeq-(n-1)I$. Substituting the weight ratios into
\cref{def:spectral-curvature} gives
\begin{align*}
 A_S^{\mu,-c}\big|_{J_S\times J_S}
 &=a^2(I+B_S)+caI
 =a^2\bigl((n+1)I+B_S\bigr)
 \succeq2a^2I.
\end{align*}
All other rows and columns vanish by downward closure. Thus both
measures have upward curvature $-c$, and we may take
$\eta=\kappa=-c$, giving $\eta+\kappa=-2c>-\delta$.
Their common support is downward closed, their rational weights
are computable in polynomial time, and
\begin{align*}
 \log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)&\le2n\log(1/a)
 =2n\log(n/c)=O(n\log n).
\end{align*}

An $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ on these instances would therefore give a
bounded-error polynomial-time test for hypergraph two-colourability.
By reducing the decision queries in the usual $\mathsf{SAT}$
self-reduction to this problem, amplifying their success probabilities,
and verifying the resulting assignment, we obtain an $\mathsf{RP}$
algorithm for $\mathsf{SAT}$. Hence $\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{RP}$.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:bit-complexity}
For rational input parameters and polynomial-time value oracles returning
rationals of polynomial encoding length, the algorithm in
\cref{thm:log-concave-convolution} has an implementation whose running time
is polynomial in the input length and $\varepsilon^{-1}$ on every execution.
Indeed, the update rule above gives $z_u=(1+1/(32n))^{k_u}$ for integers
$k_u$, and the field bound \cref{eq:balancing-bounds} implies
$\sum_u|k_u|=O(n^2B)$. Each field coordinate can therefore be stored using
polynomially many bits. The probabilities for choosing which element
to add back are ratios of sums of at most $n$ weighted oracle values,
and empirical frequencies are
ratios of sample counts. The final estimate uses products and ratios
of these numbers, fields, and powers of $t$. All these numbers have
polynomially many bits.

{We simulate the required rational probabilities using fair coin flips;
see \cite[Proposition~13]{NacuPeres2005}.}
Each binary choice can be simulated with probability at most $2^{-r}$
of requiring more than $r$ bits. If $N$ is a polynomial bound on the
total number of binary choices in the homogeneous algorithm, aborting
and returning zero when any choice needs more than
$\lceil\log_2(64N)\rceil$ bits adds at most $1/64$ to its failure
probability. The success probability proved in \cref{sec:fpras} is at
least $15/16$, so it remains above $3/4$. Conditioning, amplification,
and summation over homogeneous layers preserve polynomial bit complexity.
In particular, the rational
six-vertex instances in \cref{app:quantum} satisfy these oracle assumptions.

body_md:
Expanding $p(\mathbf1+\bm{x})$ using its nonnegative coefficients shows
that $\operatorname{supp}\widehat\mu$ is downward closed.
For $S\in\operatorname{supp}\widehat\mu$, set $q\coloneqq \partial_Sp$, so
$q(\mathbf1)=\widehat\mu(S)>0$.
As verified below, $q$ is $\alpha$-fractionally log-concave.
The coefficient ratios in \cref{def:spectral-curvature} and the
chain rule therefore give
\begin{align*}
 A_S^{\widehat\mu,\,1-\alpha^{-1}}
 &=-\nabla^2\log q(\mathbf1)
   -(1-\alpha^{-1})\operatorname{diag}(\nabla\log q(\mathbf1))\\
 &=-\alpha^{-2}
   \left.\nabla_{\bm{x}}^2\log q(x_1^\alpha,\ldots,x_n^\alpha)
   \right|_{\bm{x}=\mathbf1}\succeq0,
\end{align*}
which proves the asserted curvature bound.

It remains to verify that nonzero coordinate derivatives preserve
fractional log-concavity. We use the limiting argument of
\cite[Section~1.5]{AlimohammadiAnariShiragurVuong2021}.
Writing $\bm{x}^\alpha\coloneqq (x_1^\alpha,\ldots,x_n^\alpha)$, multiaffinity gives
\begin{align*}
 (\partial_i p)(\bm{x}^\alpha)
 &=\lim_{s\to\infty}s^{-\alpha}p\bigl((\bm{x}+s\bm{e}_i)^\alpha\bigr).
\end{align*}
Each function on the right is a positive multiple of a translate
of $\bm{x}\mapsto p(\bm{x}^\alpha)$, hence is log-concave. The log-concavity
inequality is preserved under the limit. Iterating proves the assertion
for every nonzero $\partial_Sp$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We encode the event by weighted common bases of two new matroids.
Put $m\coloneqq|{\mathcal{U}}|$, and let
${\mathcal{U}}^+=\{u^+:u\in{\mathcal{U}}\}$ and ${\mathcal{U}}^-=\{u^-:u\in{\mathcal{U}}\}$ be two
disjoint copies of ${\mathcal{U}}$. Let $\mathcal H$ be the direct sum of copies
of ${\mathcal{M}}$ and ${\mathcal{N}}^*$ on ${\mathcal{U}}^+$ and ${\mathcal{U}}^-$, respectively; it has rank $m$.
Form a bipartite graph with left vertex set
$\mathcal X\coloneqq\{x_u^0,x_u^1:u\in{\mathcal{U}}\}$ and right vertex set
${\mathcal{U}}^+\cup{\mathcal{U}}^-$. The new elements $x_u^0,x_u^1$ represent $u$ being
absent or retained, respectively. Join $x_u^0$ only to $u^-$, and join
$x_u^1$ to both $u^-$ and $u^+$.

Apply \cref{thm:rado-matroid} with $L=\mathcal X$,
$R={\mathcal{U}}^+\cup{\mathcal{U}}^-$, and $\mathcal R=\mathcal H$, and denote the
resulting matroid $\mathcal L$ by $\mathcal Q$.
A subset is independent in $\mathcal Q$
exactly when it can be matched to an independent set of $\mathcal H$.
Let $\mathcal P$ be the partition
matroid on $\mathcal X$ allowing at most one of $x_u^0,x_u^1$ for each $u$.
Both matroids have rank $m$: any basis of $\mathcal H$ can be matched
to distinct left vertices by matching $u^+$ to $x_u^1$ and $u^-$ to $x_u^0$.

The retained set $F\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}$ has the unique representation
$X_F\coloneqq\{x_u^1:u\in F\}\cup\{x_u^0:u\notin F\}$.
Since $|X_F|=m={\mathsf{rk}}(\mathcal H)$, $X_F$ is independent
in $\mathcal Q$ exactly when it can be matched to a basis of $\mathcal H$.
A matching covering $X_F$ uses {exactly one of $u^+$ and $u^-$ for each
element $u$}, so its matched right vertices form a set
$B^+\cup({\mathcal{U}}\setminus B)^-$ with
$B\subseteq F$. This set is a basis of $\mathcal H$ exactly when
$B$ is a common basis of ${\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}$. Consequently,
\[
 X_F\in{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal P)\cap{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal Q)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 F\text{ contains a common basis of }{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}.
\]
Giving $x_u^1,x_u^0$ weights $p_u,1-p_u$ makes the weighted
common-bases sum the required probability. Each $F$ is counted once,
regardless of the number of common bases it contains.

It remains to implement an independence oracle for $\mathcal Q$.
We do so by matroid intersection on restrictions and contractions
of ${\mathcal{M}}$ and ${\mathcal{N}}$. For a queried set $Y\subseteq\mathcal X$, let $S_2$
contain the elements $u$ for which both $x_u^0,x_u^1$ belong to $Y$,
let $S_0$ contain those for which neither belongs to $Y$, and let
$S_1\coloneqq\{u:x_u^1\in Y,\ x_u^0\notin Y\}$.
The possible sets of right endpoints of a matching with left endpoint set $Y$ are exactly
\[
 (S_2\cup B)^+\cup\bigl({\mathcal{U}}\setminus(S_0\cup B)\bigr)^-,
 \qquad B\subseteq S_1.
\]
Here $B$ consists of the elements $u\in S_1$ for which $x_u^1$ is matched to $u^+\in{\mathcal{U}}^+$.
By duality, the displayed set is independent in $\mathcal H$ exactly when
$S_2\cup B$ is independent in ${\mathcal{M}}$ and $S_0\cup B$ contains a basis of ${\mathcal{N}}$.

Reject if $S_2$ is dependent in ${\mathcal{M}}$. Otherwise, apply matroid intersection
to $({\mathcal{M}}/S_2)|_{S_1}$ and $({\mathcal{N}}/S_0)|_{S_1}$, and accept exactly when they have a
common independent set of size $k\coloneqq {\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}({\mathcal{U}})-{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(S_0)$,
where ${\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}$ is the rank function of ${\mathcal{N}}$.
The required oracles use only the original independence oracles:
test $I\subseteq S_1$ in ${\mathcal{M}}/S_2$ by testing $S_2\cup I$ in ${\mathcal{M}}$, and
test it in ${\mathcal{N}}/S_0$ by testing $B_0\cup I$ in ${\mathcal{N}}$, where $B_0$ is a
basis of ${\mathcal{N}}|_{S_0}$ found greedily. This gives a polynomial-time oracle for
$\mathcal Q$, so
\cref{cor:weighted-common-bases} applies.

label: lem:orientation-common-bases
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orientation-common-bases}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a loopless undirected multigraph with $|V|\ge2$, and
let $k\ge1$ be an integer. Suppose every nontrivial undirected cut
has size at least $2k$. Put $m\coloneqq|E|$, and define
\[
 {\mathcal{U}}\coloneqq\{(e,v):e\in E,\ v\in e\},
 \qquad {\mathcal{U}}_X\coloneqq\{(e,v)\in{\mathcal{U}}:v\in X\}.
\]
For an orientation $D$, let $d^-_D(v)$ be the number of edges directed
into $v$. The function
\[
 f(X)\coloneqq\max_{D\text{ a }k\text{-arc-connected orientation}}
                    \sum_{v\in X}d^-_D(v)
 \qquad(X\subseteq V)
\]
is integer-valued, monotone, and submodular, with $f(\varnothing)=0$
and $f(V)=m$. Let ${\mathcal{M}}$ be the partition matroid on ${\mathcal{U}}$ allowing
at most one incidence per edge. There is a matroid ${\mathcal{N}}$ on ${\mathcal{U}}$
with rank function
\[
 {\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(Y)=\min_{X\subseteq V}\bigl(f(X)+|Y\setminus{\mathcal{U}}_X|\bigr)
 \qquad(Y\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}).
\]
Both matroids have rank $m$, and the map
\[
 D\longmapsto A_D\coloneqq\{(e,\operatorname{head}_D(e)):e\in E\}
\]
is a bijection from the $k$-arc-connected orientations of $G$ to
${\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})\cap{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{N}})$.
head: environment
name: Common bases for strong orientations

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply \cref{cor:weighted-common-bases} to the matroids in
\cref{lem:orientation-common-bases}. First, by the orientation theorem
of Nash-Williams~\cite[Theorem~1]{NashWilliams1960Orientations},
a $k$-arc-connected orientation exists exactly when every nontrivial
undirected cut has size at least $2k$. Check this by a minimum cut,
returning zero if it fails, and put $m\coloneqq|E|$.

Give incidence $(e,v)$ weight $w_{e,v}$. The bijection in
\cref{lem:orientation-common-bases} preserves the product of weights,
so the weighted common-bases sum is exactly $Z_k(G;\bm{w})$.
It remains to implement the two independence oracles.
For ${\mathcal{M}}$, check that the queried set contains at most one incidence
per edge.

For ${\mathcal{N}}$, given any $Y\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}$, compute ${\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(Y)$ using the
lemma's rank formula and accept exactly when ${\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(Y)=|Y|$.
For fixed $Y$, the term
\[
 |Y\setminus{\mathcal{U}}_X|
   =|Y|-\sum_{v\in X}|Y\cap{\mathcal{U}}_{\{v\}}|
\]
is a constant minus a sum of fixed vertex weights. Adding it to $f(X)$
therefore preserves submodularity, so the rank formula can be evaluated
by submodular minimization~\cite{Schrijver2000SubmodularMinimization}.
To supply the required values $f(X)$, assign cost zero to directions
whose heads lie in $X$ and cost one to the others. The minimum cost
of a $k$-arc-connected orientation is $m-f(X)$, and it can be found
in polynomial time~\cite{IwataKobayashi2005Orientations}.
Thus every value query, and hence each independence query, takes
polynomial time.

With these oracles, \cref{cor:weighted-common-bases} gives the claimed
$\mathsf{FPRAS}$. If $k$ is part of the input in binary, the successful
minimum-cut test bounds $k$ by $m$, so the oracle implementations
still take polynomial time in the input length.

label: cor:weighted-euler-tours
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:weighted-euler-tours}
Let $G$ be a connected $4$-regular multigraph with nonnegative rational
weights on its local transitions. There is an $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for the
total weight of Euler tours in $G$.
head: environment
name: Weighted Euler tours

title: Proof
body_md:
{
We encode the weighted Euler tours in $G$ as weighted common bases
of two matroids and apply \cref{cor:weighted-common-bases}.
}
{
Fix an Euler tour $C$, viewed as a cyclic sequence of vertex visits.
Each vertex occurs twice because $G$ is $4$-regular. Two distinct
vertices $u,v$ \emph{alternate along $C$} if, after ignoring visits to
all other vertices, their cyclic order is $u,v,u,v$.
The \emph{interlace matrix} $A\in\mathbb F_2^{V(G)\times V(G)}$ is
defined by $A_{uv}=1$ when $u$ and $v$ alternate, and $A_{uv}=0$
otherwise; in particular, $A_{uu}=0$~\cite[p.~2]{Traldi2009BinaryNullity}.
}
{
Choose a direction for traversing $C$ and orient every edge accordingly.
At a vertex $v$, label the two incoming half-edges $a_1,a_2$ and the
two outgoing half-edges $b_1,b_2$ so that $C$ enters through $a_i$ and
leaves through $b_i$ on its $i$th visit, for $i=1,2$. Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \phi_v&\coloneqq\bigl\{\{a_1,b_1\},\{a_2,b_2\}\bigr\},\\
 \chi_v&\coloneqq\bigl\{\{a_1,b_2\},\{a_2,b_1\}\bigr\},\\
 \psi_v&\coloneqq\bigl\{\{a_1,a_2\},\{b_1,b_2\}\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Only $\phi_v$ is used by $C$. The alternative $\chi_v$ also pairs each
incoming half-edge with an outgoing half-edge, but switches which
outgoing half-edge follows each incoming one. The transition $\psi_v$
pairs the two incoming half-edges together and the two outgoing
half-edges together.
}
Associate these choices with the labeled columns
\[
 \phi_v\longleftrightarrow \bm{e}_v,\qquad
 \chi_v\longleftrightarrow \bm{A}_v,\qquad
 \psi_v\longleftrightarrow \bm{e}_v+\bm{A}_v
 \quad\text{of }[\,I\mid A\mid I+A\,]\text{ over }\mathbb F_2.
\]
For a transition choice $P$, let $K_P$ contain its selected columns.
The extended Cohn--Lempel equality
\cite[Theorem~4]{Traldi2009BinaryNullity} gives
\[
 {\#\{\text{closed trails of }P\}}=1+\operatorname{nullity}K_P.
\]
Indeed, deleting the identity choices leaves the principal interlace
matrix with a diagonal one at each $\psi$ choice, which is the matrix
in that equality. Hence $P$ is an Euler tour precisely when it is a
common basis of the column matroid and the partition matroid choosing
one column from each vertex triple. Giving each column its transition
weight preserves the weight and counts each tour once. {Gaussian
elimination and checking that at most one column is selected from each
vertex triple give the independence oracles}, so
\cref{cor:weighted-common-bases} applies.

label: def:st-linkage
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:st-linkage}
Let $G = (V,E)$ be a directed or undirected graph, and
let $S,T\subseteq V$ be disjoint terminal sets with $|S|=|T|=k\ge1$.
An \emph{$S$--$T$ linkage} consists of $k$ paths that share no vertices.
Each path joins a vertex of $S$ to a vertex of $T$, and every vertex of
$S$ and $T$ is used as an endpoint exactly once. We do not specify which
vertex of $S$ is joined to which vertex of $T$. If $G$ is directed,
all paths must follow edge directions from $S$ to $T$.

name: $S$--$T$ linkage

title: Corollary

name: $S$--$T$ Network reliability

title: Remark
body_md:
Taking $S=\{s\}$ and $T=\{t\}$ in an undirected graph recovers
the $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for $s$--$t$ reliability in \cite{FengFuGuo2026} with worse running time.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first encode directed linkage as the existence of a perfect matching
in a random bipartite graph, then apply
\cref{lem:common-basis-availability}. An undirected edge gadget gives
the undirected case.

For a directed graph, discard loops, arcs entering $S$, and arcs leaving
$T$. Form a bipartite graph with vertex classes
\begin{align*}
 V_L&\coloneqq \{\ell_v:v\in V\setminus T\},&
 V_R&\coloneqq \{r_v:v\in V\setminus S\}.
\end{align*}
{Replace each remaining arc $u\to v$ by the edge $\ell_ur_v$.
Keep this edge with the same probability as the original arc.}
Add an always-present edge $\ell_vr_v$ for
each $v\notin S\cup T$. A linkage gives a perfect matching by selecting
its path edges and the diagonal edges at unused vertices. Conversely,
following a perfect matching from each source reaches a distinct sink:
entering a cycle or another source's path would give a vertex two selected
incoming edges. Thus, for every {retained edge set},
\begin{align*}
 \text{the directed graph admits an $S$--$T$ linkage}
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \text{the bipartite graph has a perfect matching}.
\end{align*}

Let ${\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}$ be the partition matroids on the bipartite edge set,
allowing at most one edge at each left and right endpoint, respectively.
If the full bipartite graph has no perfect matching, return zero.
Otherwise both matroids have rank $|V|-k$, and a retained edge set
contains a perfect matching exactly when it contains a common basis.
Thus \cref{lem:common-basis-availability} approximates the desired
probability, including the always-present diagonal edges.

Finally, for an undirected edge $e=\{u,v\}$, introduce new vertices
$a_e,b_e$ and arcs
\begin{align*}
 u\to a_e,\quad v\to a_e,\quad a_e\to b_e,\quad
 b_e\to u,\quad b_e\to v.
\end{align*}
Only $a_e\to b_e$ is random, with retention probability $p_e$; the
other four arcs are always present. Vertex-disjoint undirected paths
lift to vertex-disjoint directed paths. Conversely, simple directed
paths project to vertex-disjoint undirected paths, since {returning
through the gadget to the vertex where the path entered would repeat
that vertex}. This preserves
the linkage event for every {choice of retained original edges} and uses one independent
random variable per original edge. The directed result therefore also
proves the undirected case.

title: Proof
body_md:
We express the event as containment of a common basis and apply
\cref{lem:common-basis-availability}.
Delete loops and arcs entering $r$, which do not affect this event.
The one-vertex case has probability one. Otherwise put
$q\coloneqq k(|V|-1)$, and return zero if $q>|E|$.
Let ${\mathcal{M}}$ be the union of $k$ copies of the graphic matroid of the
underlying undirected multigraph.
{A set is independent in ${\mathcal{M}}$ exactly when it can be
partitioned into $k$ forests after ignoring the arc directions.}
Let ${\mathcal{N}}$ be the partition
matroid allowing at most $k$ arcs entering each nonroot vertex.
{The polynomial-time matroid-union algorithm
\cite[Section~4.1]{BercziFrank2010Packing} gives an independence oracle
for ${\mathcal{M}}$, using cycle detection to test independence in each graphic
matroid. For ${\mathcal{N}}$, we count the queried arcs entering each nonroot
vertex and check that every count is at most $k$.}
If either rank is less than $q$, the event is impossible; otherwise
both ranks equal $q$.

{
For each $F\subseteq E$, we have
\[
 \Lambda(V,F)_{r,v}\ge k\ \text{for all }v\ne r
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 F\text{ contains a common basis of }{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}.
\]
Edmonds's arborescence-packing theorem
\cite{Edmonds1973EdgeDisjointBranchings}
(see also \cite[Theorem~1.1]{BercziFrank2010Packing}) equates the
left-hand condition with the existence in $F$ of $k$ arc-disjoint
spanning out-arborescences rooted at $r$, that is, directed spanning
trees in which $r$ reaches every vertex. The standard matroid
representation \cite[Section~4.1]{BercziFrank2010Packing} identifies
the unions of $k$ such arborescences with the common bases of
${\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}$.
\par
}

Applying \cref{lem:common-basis-availability} now gives the claimed
approximation. The preliminary bound $k(|V|-1)\le|E|$ ensures
polynomial size even when $k$ is given in binary.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:determinantal-applications}
There is an $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for each of the following quantities:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item For a rational positive semidefinite matrix $L$ indexed by
 ${\mathcal{U}}$ and a matroid ${\mathcal{M}}$ on ${\mathcal{U}}$ given by an independence oracle,
 \[
  Z_{{\mathcal{M}}}(L)\coloneqq\sum_{S\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})}\det L[S].
 \]
 \item For rational positive semidefinite matrices $A,B$ indexed by
 the same set ${\mathcal{U}}$,
 \[
  Z(A,B)\coloneqq\sum_{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\det A[S]\det B[S].
 \]
 \item For rational positive semidefinite $d\times d$ matrices
 $A_1,\ldots,A_d$, the mixed discriminant
 \[
  \Delta(A_1,\ldots,A_d)
  \coloneqq[x_1\cdots x_d]\det\left(\sum_{i=1}^d x_iA_i\right).
 \]
\end{enumerate}

label: prop:cauchy-binet
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:cauchy-binet}
Let $A\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ and $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$,
where $n\ge d$. For $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|=d$, let $A_{:,S}$
be the $d\times d$ matrix formed by the columns of $A$ indexed by
$S$, and let $B_{S,:}$ be the $d\times d$ matrix formed by the
rows of $B$ indexed by $S$, both in increasing order. Then
\[
 \det(AB)=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq[n]\\|S|=d}}
                 \det(A_{:,S})\det(B_{S,:}).
\]
head: environment
name: Cauchy--Binet formula

title: Proof
body_md:
The first two reductions use the principal-minor identities
{(see \cite[Section~3.2]{BorceaBrandenLiggett2009})}
\begin{align*}
 p_L(\bm{x})\coloneqq\sum_S\det L[S]\bm{x}^S
   &={\det(I+LD_{\bm{x}})=}\det(I+L^{1/2}D_{\bm{x}}L^{1/2}),\\
 q_L(\bm{x})\coloneqq\sum_T\det L[{\mathcal{U}}\setminus T]\bm{x}^T
   &=\det(L+D_{\bm{x}}),
\end{align*}
where $D_{\bm{x}}\coloneqq\operatorname{diag}(\bm{x})$.
{
To obtain the first expansion, use multilinearity of the determinant
in its columns: choosing columns from $LD_{\bm{x}}$ at indices in $S$ and
from $I$ elsewhere contributes $\det L[S]\bm{x}^S$.
Similarly, choosing columns from $D_{\bm{x}}$ at indices in $T$ and from
$L$ elsewhere contributes $\det L[{\mathcal{U}}\setminus T]\bm{x}^T$, giving the
second expansion.
The last equality for $p_L$ follows from Sylvester's identity
$\det(I+AB)=\det(I+BA)$.
}

{
Both polynomials are log-concave. Indeed, the matrices
$I+L^{1/2}D_{\bm{x}}L^{1/2}$ and $L+D_{\bm{x}}$ are affine functions of $\bm{x}$
and positive definite when $\bm{x}>\mathbf0$, even if $L$ is singular.
The function $X\mapsto\log\det X$ is concave on positive definite
matrices \cite[Section~3.1.5, p.~74]{BoydVandenberghe2004}.
Composing a concave function with an affine map preserves concavity,
so $\log p_L(\bm{x})$ and $\log q_L(\bm{x})$ are concave.
\par
}

For Item~1, apply \cref{lem:matroid-constraint} with
$\omega(S)\coloneqq\det L[S]$, initialized at $\varnothing$.

For Item~2, use
\[
 Z(A,B)=[\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]\bigl(p_A(\bm{x})q_B(\bm{x})\bigr)
\]
and apply \cref{thm:log-concave-convolution}, with initial sets
$\varnothing$ and ${\mathcal{U}}$. This is the normalizing constant for the
product of two DPPs \cite{OhsakaMatsuoka2021}; dividing by
$\det(I+A)\det(I+B)$ gives their agreement probability.

For Item~3, use the partition-matroid reduction of
\cite[Section~4.1]{CelisEtAl2017}. Rational $LDL^{\mathsf T}$
decompositions give
$A_i=\sum_{e\in E_i}c_e\bm{v}_e\bm{v}_e^{\mathsf T}$ with $c_e>0$
and $|E_i|\le d$. {Here $E_i$ indexes the rank-one terms
of $A_i$; we take these index sets to be pairwise disjoint.
If $E_i=\varnothing$ for some $i$, then $A_i=0$ and $\Delta=0$.
Otherwise put $E\coloneqq\bigcup_{i=1}^d E_i$, let $V$ have columns
$\bm{v}_e$, and let ${\mathcal{M}}$ be the partition matroid on $E$ whose bases contain exactly one
element from each $E_i$. Thus a basis selects one rank-one term
from each matrix $A_i$.}

{
To compute the coefficient defining $\Delta$, let $D(\bm{x})$ be the
diagonal matrix indexed by $E$ with $D(\bm{x})_{e,e}=c_ex_i$ for
$e\in E_i$. Then $\sum_{i=1}^d x_iA_i=VD(\bm{x})V^{\mathsf T}$.
For $S\subseteq E$ with $|S|=d$, write $V_S$ for the $d\times d$
matrix formed by the columns of $V$ indexed by $S$.
Applying \cref{prop:cauchy-binet} with $A=VD(\bm{x})$ and
$B=V^{\mathsf T}$ gives
\[
 \det\left(\sum_{i=1}^d x_iA_i\right)
 =\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq E\\|S|=d}}
   \det(V_S)^2\left(\prod_{e\in S}c_e\right)
   \prod_{i=1}^d x_i^{|S\cap E_i|}.
\]
Here $\det(V_S)^2=\det(V_S^{\mathsf T}V_S)
=\det((V^{\mathsf T}V)[S])$.
The monomial $\prod_{i=1}^d x_i^{|S\cap E_i|}$ equals
$x_1\cdots x_d$ exactly when $S$ contains one element of each
$E_i$, that is, when $S$ is a basis of ${\mathcal{M}}$.
Extracting this coefficient therefore gives
}
\[
 \Delta(A_1,\ldots,A_d)
 =\sum_{S\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})}\det((V^{\mathsf T}V)[S])\prod_{e\in S}c_e.
\]
Apply \cref{lem:matroid-constraint} to this determinant weight:
the factors $c_e$ are external fields, so log-concavity persists,
and $\varnothing$ is again an initial set.
All coefficient queries and decompositions use rational arithmetic
of polynomial bit length. The square roots in $p_L$ serve only to
prove log-concavity.

title: Remark
body_md:
An Eulerian orientation specifies the direction of each edge, with
equal indegree and outdegree at every vertex. If $G$ is connected,
this guarantees the existence of a directed Euler tour; otherwise,
each connected component admits one. The six-vertex partition
function includes one term per orientation, regardless of how many
directed Euler tours it admits.

The Euler-tour weights in \cref{app:euler-tours} depend on the
whole pairing of the four incident half-edges, whereas the
six-vertex weights depend only on the incoming pair. For example,
if edges $1,2$ enter a vertex and $3,4$ leave it, the compatible
local pairings
\[
 \bigl\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\bigr\}
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \bigl\{\{1,4\},\{2,3\}\bigr\}
\]
may receive different transition weights in \cref{app:euler-tours}.
Both have incoming pair $\{1,2\}$ under this orientation, so the
six-vertex weight is $a_v$ in either case.

label: cor:six-vertex
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:six-vertex}
For every loopless $4$-regular multigraph $G$, there is an
$\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for its six-vertex partition function when the local
{pair weights $a_v,b_v,c_v$} are nonnegative rationals satisfying
\[
 a_v\le b_v+c_v,\qquad b_v\le a_v+c_v,\qquad c_v\le a_v+b_v
 \quad\text{for every }v\in V(G).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Use the incidences ${\mathcal{U}}\coloneqq\{(v,e):v\in e\}$ as the ground set,
and let ${\mathcal{M}}$ be the partition matroid choosing one incidence of each
edge. Assign to $S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}$ the product of its local incoming-pair
weights, with weight zero unless $S$ has two incidences at every vertex.
Then bases of ${\mathcal{M}}$ with positive weight are exactly the six-vertex
orientations, with their prescribed weights. We apply
\cref{lem:matroid-constraint} to this weight.

Its generating polynomial is $\prod_vq_v$, where
\[
 q_v(\bm{x})=a_v(x_1x_2+x_3x_4)+b_v(x_1x_3+x_2x_4)
                  +c_v(x_1x_4+x_2x_3).
\]
An all-zero local triple gives partition function zero.
Otherwise the Hessian of $q_v$ has eigenvalues
$a_v+b_v+c_v$, $a_v-b_v-c_v$, $-a_v+b_v-c_v$, and
$-a_v-b_v+c_v$. The triangle inequalities leave at most one positive
eigenvalue, which is the log-concavity criterion for a nonzero
homogeneous quadratic with nonnegative coefficients
\cite[Section~2]{BrandenHuh2020}. Hence the product is log-concave.
Choosing any positive incoming pair at each vertex gives an initial
set, and coefficient queries are products of the given local weights.
Thus \cref{lem:matroid-constraint} applies, {including equality
in the triangle inequalities}.

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply \cref{lem:matroid-constraint} on the set
${\mathcal{U}}\coloneqq[p]\times E$ of ordered pairs $(i,e)$: the first entry
$i\in[p]$ is a player index, and the second entry $e\in E$ is an element.
Including $(i,e)$ records that player $i$ uses element $e$.
Let ${\mathcal{M}}$ be the matroid whose bases are precisely
$\{(i,e):1\le i\le p,\ e\in B_i\}$ as each $B_i$ ranges over the bases of ${\mathcal{M}}_i$.
Thus its rank is $R\coloneqq\sum_i{\mathsf{rk}}({\mathcal{M}}_i)$.
Put $V_e\coloneqq[p]\times\{e\}$ and define
\[
 \omega(X)\coloneqq\mathbf{1}[|X|=R]\prod_e a_e(|X\cap V_e|).
\]
Each basis of ${\mathcal{M}}$ specifies one profile, so
$Z(a)=\sum_{X\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})}\omega(X)$.

To show that the generating polynomial of $\omega$ is log-concave,
we use the following sufficient condition
\cite[Corollary~3.16 and Theorem~2.30]{BrandenHuh2020}:
for every $X,Y$ with $\omega(X),\omega(Y)>0$ and every
$a\in X\setminus Y$, some $b\in Y\setminus X$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:congestion-exchange}
 \omega(X)\omega(Y)\le\omega(X-a+b)\omega(Y+a-b).
\end{equation}
Here $X-a+b$ means $(X\setminus\{a\})\cup\{b\}$, and similarly for $Y+a-b$.
The sets $X,Y$ in this condition need only have positive $\omega$-weight;
they are not required to be bases of ${\mathcal{M}}$.
For each element $g\in E$, write $x_g=|X\cap V_g|$ and $y_g=|Y\cap V_g|$.
                                                                       
Fix $a \in V_e$ for some element $e$.
If $x_e\le y_e$, the fact that $a\in(X\setminus Y)\cap V_e$ gives
\[
 |(Y\setminus X)\cap V_e|
 =y_e-x_e+|(X\setminus Y)\cap V_e|\ge1.
\]
Thus we can choose $b\in(Y\setminus X)\cap V_e$ simply by counting;
no matroid property is needed. Exchanging $a$ and $b$ leaves every
load unchanged, so $\omega(X-a+b)=\omega(X)$ and
$\omega(Y+a-b)=\omega(Y)$.
Otherwise $x_e>y_e$. Since
$\sum_g x_g=|X|=|Y|=\sum_g y_g$, there must be a different element
$f\ne e$ with $x_f<y_f$. Choose $b\in(Y\setminus X)\cap V_f$.
Since $V_f=[p]\times\{f\}$, the first entry of $b$ is a player index
and its second entry is the fixed element $f$. This choice is possible
because $Y$ contains more pairs in $V_f$ than $X$.
Exchanging $a$ and $b$ changes the loads at $e$ from $(x_e,y_e)$ to
$(x_e-1,y_e+1)$, and at $f$ from $(x_f,y_f)$ to $(x_f+1,y_f-1)$.
These loads stay within their allowed intervals, and the log-concavity
of $a_e,a_f$ gives \cref{eq:congestion-exchange}.

To find a set of positive weight, choose integers $k_e\in[l_e,u_e]$ with
$\sum_e k_e=R$ and select $k_e$ elements from each $V_e$. Such integers exist
exactly when $\sum_e l_e\le R\le\sum_e u_e$; otherwise $Z(a)=0$.
We evaluate $\omega(X)$ by checking $|X|=R$, counting $|X\cap V_e|$
for each element, and multiplying the corresponding weights.
The ratio of its largest
to smallest positive weight satisfies
\[
 {\mathcal{R}}_\omega\le\prod_e
     \frac{\max_{l_e\le k\le u_e}a_e(k)}
          {\min_{l_e\le k\le u_e}a_e(k)}.
\]
Thus \cref{lem:matroid-constraint} applies.

$c_e(1)\le\cdots\le c_e(p)$ and $\beta\ge0$ specified above,
restrict the profiles $B$ to those satisfying
$l_e\le\ell_e(B)\le u_e$ for every $e\in E$.
{A randomized algorithm returns an estimate of $Z(a)$ with
relative error at most $\varepsilon$}, with probability at least $3/4$, in the form
$\bigl(\prod_e\max_k a_e(k)\bigr)\widehat Z$, where $\widehat Z$ is
rational and the exponential factor is specified by its exact rational
exponent. If $Z(a)>0$, there is also a sampler
within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the Gibbs distribution.
The running times are polynomial in $pq$, the input encoding length,
$\varepsilon^{-1}$, and the \emph{numerical} value of $\Lambda$.
If the costs are nonnegative and every $l_e=0$, then
$\max_k a_e(k)=a_e(0)=1$ for every $e$, so the estimate is rational.

title: Proof
body_md:
{
It suffices to approximate the partition function and sample after
dividing each table by its largest entry. Indeed, put
\[
 \bar a_e(k)\coloneqq\frac{a_e(k)}{\max_j a_e(j)}.
\]
This leaves the Gibbs distribution unchanged, and
$Z(a)=\bigl(\prod_e\max_k a_e(k)\bigr)Z(\bar a)$.
The logarithm of this factor is rational and can be computed exactly
from the given costs. We replace $\bar a_e$ by rational log-concave
tables with nearly the same weights. For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, set
$\tau\coloneqq\varepsilon/[64q(p+1)^2]$ and $r\coloneqq1+\tau$.
For each $l_e\le k\le u_e$, write $\bar a_e(k)=e^{-x}$, where
$x=-\log\bar a_e(k)\in[0,\Lambda]$ is rational and computable exactly
from the costs. Standard algorithms for evaluating the exponential
function \cite[Sections~4.3--4.4]{BrentZimmermann2010} compute a
positive rational approximation $\widetilde a_e(k)$ satisfying
\[
 \left|\log\frac{\widetilde a_e(k)}{\bar a_e(k)}\right|\le\tau/16
\]
in time polynomial in the input encoding length, $\Lambda$, and
$\log(\tau^{-1})$.
\par}
{The rational approximation may lose log-concavity.
To ensure log-concavity, we make a further small adjustment: define}
$b_e(k)\coloneqq\widetilde a_e(k)r^{-k^2}$ on the allowed interval
and zero outside it. For every $l_e<k<u_e$,
\[
 \log\frac{b_e(k)^2}{b_e(k-1)b_e(k+1)}
 \ge2\log r-\tau/4>0.
\]
Thus $b_e$ is log-concave, and every profile $B$
{with $l_e\le\ell_e(B)\le u_e$ for every $e\in E$} obeys
\[
 {\left|\log\frac{\prod_e b_e(\ell_e(B))}{\prod_e \bar a_e(\ell_e(B))}\right|}
 \le q\tau/16+qp^2\log r\le\varepsilon/64.
\]
Consequently the sums $Z(b)$ and {$Z(\bar a)$} differ by a factor at most
$e^{\varepsilon/64}$ in either direction. When these sums are positive,
dividing the profile weights by their respective sums gives two
probability distributions whose total variation distance is at most
$e^{\varepsilon/32}-1<\varepsilon/16$.
Applying \cref{cor:congestion-tables} with accuracy $\varepsilon/4$
{{gives an estimate of $Z(\bar a)$ with relative error at most $\varepsilon$.}
Multiplying by $\prod_e\max_k a_e(k)$ gives the required estimate of $Z(a)$.}
For sampling, decide for each pair $(i,e)$ whether $e\in B_i$, using
approximate counts to estimate the total weight of each choice
\cite{JVV1986}. Fixing these choices deletes or contracts elements of
the player matroids. For each element, it also shifts the load index
by the number of players already required to use it and removes
infeasible entries. The resulting tables remain log-concave, so
\cref{cor:congestion-tables} applies at every step.
Sampling from the distribution defined by the rational
tables $b_e$ within total variation distance $\varepsilon/4$ then gives
the desired approximate Gibbs sample.
The rational tables have encoding length polynomial in $\Lambda$, the
input encoding length, and $\varepsilon^{-1}$, which gives the stated
running time.

label: prop:integer-weight-intersection
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:integer-weight-intersection}
Let $\bm{c}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}^m$ be given in \emph{unary}, meaning
that each $c_i$ is represented by $c_i$ copies of the symbol $1$.
Let $\mu,\nu:[\bm{0},\bm{c}]\cap\mathbb Z^m\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$
be log-$\mathrm M$-concave weights, extended by zero outside the box,
given by evaluation oracles. Suppose we are given initial vectors
$\bm{x}_0,\bm{y}_0$ with $\mu(\bm{x}_0)>0$ and $\nu(\bm{y}_0)>0$,
and upper bounds on their coefficient ranges whose logarithms are
polynomial in the input length. Then there is an $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for
\begin{align*}
 Z\coloneqq\sum_{\bm{k}\in[\bm{0},\bm{c}]\cap\mathbb Z^m}
                   \mu(\bm{k})\nu(\bm{k})
\end{align*}
in the arithmetic model of \cref{thm:log-concave-convolution}.
In particular, membership
oracles and one point in each of two $\mathrm M$-convex families
$\mathcal A,\mathcal D$ in the box suffice to approximate
$|\mathcal A\cap\mathcal D|$.
head: environment
name: Counting weighted intersections of integer families

title: Proof
body_md:
We construct two subset weights whose convolution is $Z/\bm{c}!$,
where $\bm{k}!\coloneqq\prod_i k_i!$. We then show that their
generating polynomials are log-concave and apply
\cref{thm:log-concave-convolution}.
If the coordinate sums of the two initial vectors differ, the
supports are disjoint and $Z=0$, so assume these sums agree.

\emph{Encoding the integer vectors.}
Take disjoint sets ${\mathcal{U}}_i$ with $|{\mathcal{U}}_i|=c_i$ and put
${\mathcal{U}}\coloneqq\bigsqcup_i{\mathcal{U}}_i$. For $S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}$, write
$k_i(S)\coloneqq|S\cap{\mathcal{U}}_i|$ and define
\begin{align}
 \widehat\mu(S)
 &\coloneqq\mu(\bm{k}(S))\frac{(\bm{c}-\bm{k}(S))!}{\bm{c}!},
 \label{eq:integer-clone-weights}\\
 \widehat\nu(S)
 &\coloneqq\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{k}(S))\frac{(\bm{c}-\bm{k}(S))!}{\bm{c}!}.
 \notag
\end{align}
In the convolution, $\widehat\mu(S)$ and
$\widehat\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)$ use the same integer vector
$\bm{k}(S)$. Exactly
$\binom{\bm{c}}{\bm{k}}\coloneqq\prod_i\binom{c_i}{k_i}$
subsets encode $\bm{k}$, and the factorial weights cancel this
multiplicity:
\begin{align}\label{eq:integer-convolution-identity}
 (\widehat\mu*\widehat\nu)({\mathcal{U}})
 &=\sum_{\bm{0}\le\bm{k}\le\bm{c}}
   \binom{\bm{c}}{\bm{k}}\mu(\bm{k})\nu(\bm{k})
   \frac{(\bm{c}-\bm{k})!\,\bm{k}!}{(\bm{c}!)^2}
   =\frac{Z}{\bm{c}!}.
\end{align}

\emph{Log-concavity of the generating polynomials.}
We use the weighted exchange condition in \cref{eq:integer-weight-exchange}
for $\nu$; log-concavity of its generating polynomial alone would not
provide this condition. Put
$\bar\nu(\bm{k})\coloneqq\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{k})$ for integer vectors
$\bm{k}$ satisfying $0\le k_i\le c_i$ for every $i$, and set
$\bar\nu(\bm{k})=0$ otherwise. We first verify that $\bar\nu$ is
also log-$\mathrm M$-concave.
Take $\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\operatorname{supp}\bar\nu$ with $x_i>y_i$.
Then $\bm{c}-\bm{y},\bm{c}-\bm{x}\in\operatorname{supp}\nu$ and
$(\bm{c}-\bm{y})_i>(\bm{c}-\bm{x})_i$. Apply
\cref{eq:integer-weight-exchange} to these two vectors in this order.
It gives an index $j$ with
$(\bm{c}-\bm{y})_j<(\bm{c}-\bm{x})_j$, equivalently $x_j<y_j$, and
\begin{align*}
 \bar\nu(\bm{x})\bar\nu(\bm{y})
 &=\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{y})\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{x})\\
 &\le\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{y}-\bm{e}_i+\bm{e}_j)
       \nu(\bm{c}-\bm{x}+\bm{e}_i-\bm{e}_j)\\
 &=\bar\nu(\bm{x}-\bm{e}_i+\bm{e}_j)
   \bar\nu(\bm{y}+\bm{e}_i-\bm{e}_j).
\end{align*}
Moreover, if the vectors in $\operatorname{supp}\nu$ have coordinate sum $r$,
then those in $\operatorname{supp}\bar\nu$ have coordinate sum $\sum_i c_i-r$.
Thus $\bar\nu$ satisfies both parts of the definition.

By \cite[Corollary~3.16]{BrandenHuh2020}, the exponential generating
polynomial of a log-$\mathrm M$-concave weight is Lorentzian.
Applying this separately to $\mu$ and $\bar\nu$ gives two Lorentzian
polynomials:
\begin{align*}
 g_\mu^{\mathrm{exp}}(\bm{x})
 &\coloneqq\sum_{\bm{0}\le\bm{k}\le\bm{c}}
       \frac{\mu(\bm{k})}{\bm{k}!}\bm{x}^{\bm{k}},\\
 g_{\bar\nu}^{\mathrm{exp}}(\bm{x})
 &\coloneqq\sum_{\bm{0}\le\bm{k}\le\bm{c}}
       \frac{\bar\nu(\bm{k})}{\bm{k}!}\bm{x}^{\bm{k}}
 =\sum_{\bm{0}\le\bm{k}\le\bm{c}}
       \frac{\nu(\bm{k})}{(\bm{c}-\bm{k})!}\bm{x}^{\bm{c}-\bm{k}}.
\end{align*}
{Apply polarization from
\cref{app:weight-background}, with the new variables for coordinate $i$
indexed by ${\mathcal{U}}_i$. Since
$1/(k!\binom{c_i}{k})=(c_i-k)!/c_i!$, the resulting polynomials are
exactly $g_{\widehat\mu}$ and $g_{\widehat\nu}$ from
\cref{eq:integer-clone-weights}.} These are multiaffine log-concave
polynomials because polarization preserves the Lorentzian property
\cite[Proposition~3.1 and Theorem~2.30]{BrandenHuh2020}.

\emph{Oracle access and running time.}
Choose $S_0,T_0\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}$ with
$|S_0\cap{\mathcal{U}}_i|=(x_0)_i$ and
$|T_0\cap{\mathcal{U}}_i|=c_i-(y_0)_i$ for every $i$. These satisfy
$\widehat\mu(S_0)>0$ and $\widehat\nu(T_0)>0$.
The input length is at least $\sum_i c_i=|{\mathcal{U}}|$ under the stated
encoding. Factorials can be precomputed and
{the weights $\widehat\mu$ and $\widehat\nu$} evaluated in polynomial time. Their coefficient
ranges increase by at most a factor of $\bm{c}!$, whose logarithm
is also polynomial in the input length.
Apply \cref{thm:log-concave-convolution} and multiply the estimate by
$\bm{c}!$, using \cref{eq:integer-convolution-identity}, to obtain the
claimed $\mathsf{FPRAS}$.

label: cor:weighted-contingency-tables
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Contingency tables with log-concave entry weights

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply \cref{prop:integer-weight-intersection} to the intersection
of the row-sum family and the column-sum family, assigning all entry
weights to the first family.

First, find a table with positive weight, or certify that
$Z_{\bm{r},\bm{c}}=0$. This is a standard integral-flow feasibility
problem on the bipartite graph of rows and columns: the edge $(i,j)$
carries $X_{ij}$, its lower and upper bounds are the endpoints of the
positive interval of $w_{ij}$, and the required totals at the row and
column vertices are $\bm{r}$ and $\bm{c}$. It can be solved in
polynomial time. Assume henceforth that such a table $X_0$ exists.
If all $u_{ij}=0$, evaluate the single possible table directly.
Otherwise, regard matrices as vectors of the entries with $u_{ij}>0$;
the omitted entries remain fixed at zero.

Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal D$ be the families satisfying
$0\le X_{ij}\le u_{ij}$ and, respectively, the row sums and the
column sums. Both are $\mathrm M$-convex. Indeed, if $X_{ij}>Y_{ij}$,
the equal sum in that row (respectively, column) gives another entry
where $X$ is smaller than $Y$. Exchanging one unit between these two
entries in opposite directions in $X$ and $Y$ preserves the required
sums and entry bounds. Set
\begin{align*}
 \mu(X)&\coloneqq\mathbf{1}_{\{X\in\mathcal A\}}
                  \prod_{i=1}^m\prod_{j=1}^n w_{ij}(X_{ij}),
 &\nu(X)&\coloneqq\mathbf{1}_{\{X\in\mathcal D\}}.
\end{align*}
{The preceding observation about products of coordinate weights shows}
that these weights
are log-$\mathrm M$-concave, with coefficient ranges at most $R$ and
$1$. Their evaluations take polynomial time, and $X_0$ has positive
weight under both. Their inner product is $Z_{\bm{r},\bm{c}}$.
The coordinate upper bounds have polynomial sum, so they can be
represented in unary. Thus \cref{prop:integer-weight-intersection}
gives the claimed $\mathsf{FPRAS}$.

label: cor:bounded-integer-flows
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Bounded integer flows

title: Proof
body_md:
We give a weight-preserving bijection between flows and contingency
tables, then apply \cref{cor:weighted-contingency-tables}.
Write $D\coloneqq\sum_a d_a$ for the total flow capacity.
If $\sum_v h_v\ne0$, there is no feasible flow, so return zero.

\emph{From flows to square matrices.}
We construct an $N\times N$ nonnegative integer matrix $X$, where
$N=|V|+|E|$ and the rows and columns are indexed by the disjoint union
$V\sqcup E$. Giving each edge its own index keeps parallel edges and
loops distinct. The required row sums $R_i$ and column sums $C_i$ are
\begin{align*}
 R_v&\coloneqq\sum_{a\text{ out of }v}d_a,
 &C_v&\coloneqq R_v-h_v &&(v\in V),\\
 R_a&\coloneqq d_a,
 &C_a&\coloneqq d_a &&(a\in E).
\end{align*}
If any $C_v<0$, return zero: a feasible flow would satisfy
$h_v\le\sum_{a\text{ out of }v}q_a\le R_v$.
The row and column sums are now nonnegative and satisfy
$\sum_iR_i=\sum_iC_i=2D$.
Given a flow $\bm{q}$, start with $X=0$ and set
\begin{align*}
 X_{u,a}=X_{a,v}&\coloneqq q_a,
 &X_{a,a}&\coloneqq d_a-q_a &&(a=u\to v),\\
 X_{v,v}&\coloneqq R_v-\sum_{a\text{ out of }v}q_a
 && &&(v\in V).
\end{align*}
All entries not assigned above remain zero. In particular,
\begin{align*}
 X_{u,v}&=0 &&(u,v\in V,\ u\ne v),\\
 X_{a,b}&=0 &&(a,b\in E,\ a\ne b).
\end{align*}
For an edge $a=u\to v$, the mixed entries also satisfy
$X_{w,a}=0$ for $w\in V\setminus\{u\}$ and
$X_{a,w}=0$ for $w\in V\setminus\{v\}$.
Allow each of
$X_{u,a},X_{a,v},X_{a,a}$ to lie in $[0,d_a]$, and each $X_{v,v}$
to lie in $[0,R_v]$. These bounds hold for the matrix just constructed,
and flow conservation gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{j\in V\sqcup E}X_{i,j}=R_i,\qquad
 \sum_{j\in V\sqcup E}X_{j,i}=C_i
 \qquad(i\in V\sqcup E).
\end{align*}
Conversely, consider a matrix with these entry bounds, fixed zero
entries, and row and column sums. For each edge $a=u\to v$, its row
and column equations give
\begin{align*}
 X_{a,v}+X_{a,a}=d_a=X_{u,a}+X_{a,a},
\end{align*}
so $X_{u,a}=X_{a,v}$ defines a unique flow $q_a$.
Subtracting the column equation at vertex $v$ from its row equation
gives outgoing flow minus incoming flow equal to $R_v-C_v=h_v$.
All diagonal entries are then uniquely determined, proving the
bijection.

\emph{Applying the contingency-table result.}
Assign weight $w_a(X_{u,a})$ to the entry $X_{u,a}$ and weight one
to the other entries. The bijection preserves weights, and every
entry-weight table is log-concave with interval support. The product
of their coefficient ranges is $R$, and their upper bounds sum to
\begin{align*}
 3\sum_{a\in E}d_a+\sum_{v\in V}R_v=4D.
\end{align*}
Thus \cref{cor:weighted-contingency-tables} gives an
$\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for $Z_{\bm{h}}$.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:network-polytope-vertices}

with running time polynomial in the input length and $\varepsilon^{-1}$
in the arithmetic model of \cref{thm:log-concave-convolution}.

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We recall the reduction of Guo and Jerrum
\cite[Section~4]{NetworkGuoJerrum2023} and apply
\cref{cor:bounded-integer-flows} with unit weights. We verify the
bijection from vertices to flows and bound the total capacity in
terms of the dimensions of $A$.

The vertices of $P$ are exactly its binary points. For each such point
$\bm{x}$, set $\bm{y}=A\bm{x}$. The identity $A=B_T^{-1}B_E$ gives
\begin{align*}
 \bm{y}=A\bm{x}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 B_T\bm{y}-B_E\bm{x}=\bm{0}.
\end{align*}
For each labeled edge $e=(u\to v)\in E$, let
$\overleftarrow e=(v\to u)$ denote the same edge with its direction
reversed, and set $\overleftarrow E\coloneqq\{\overleftarrow e:e\in E\}$.
On the graph with edge set
$E(T)\sqcup\overleftarrow E$, write $f_a$ for the flow on edge $a$:
set $f_t=y_t$ on each tree edge and $f_{\overleftarrow e}=x_e$
on the reversal of each edge $e\in E$. The equation on the right
expresses \emph{flow conservation}: total outgoing flow equals total
incoming flow at each vertex whose row appears in the matrices,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{a\text{ out of }v}f_a
 =\sum_{a\text{ into }v}f_a
 \qquad(v\in V\setminus\{r\}).
\end{align*}
Here $r$ is the vertex whose row was deleted when defining $B_T$ and
$B_E$ above. The same equality also holds at $r$: every edge contributes
once to an outgoing sum and once to an incoming sum, so the sum of
outgoing minus incoming flow over all vertices is zero. Since this
difference vanishes at every $v\ne r$, it must vanish at $r$ as well.
The tree flows are uniquely determined by $\bm{x}$, so this is a
bijection between vertices of $P$ and integer flows satisfying
$\ell_t\le y_t\le u_t$ and $0\le x_e\le1$.

We next shift the tree flows to make all flows nonnegative and bound
their capacities. Let $a_t^+,a_t^-$ count the $+1,-1$ entries in row $t$
of $A$. Since $y_t=(A\bm{x})_t$, every binary $\bm{x}$ satisfies
$-a_t^-\le y_t\le a_t^+$. We may therefore replace the original
constraint $\ell_t\le y_t\le u_t$ on the flow through tree edge $t$
by $L_t\le y_t\le U_t$, without changing the feasible flows, where
\begin{align*}
 L_t\coloneqq\max\{\ell_t,-a_t^-\},\qquad
 U_t\coloneqq\min\{u_t,a_t^+\}.
\end{align*}
If any $L_t>U_t$, the count is zero. Otherwise put
$q_t=y_t-L_t$ on tree edges and $q_e=x_e$ on reversed edges.
Let $B$ be the full vertex-edge incidence matrix of this graph, with outgoing
entries $+1$ and incoming entries $-1$. The equivalent constraints are
\begin{align*}
 B\bm{q}=\bm{h},\qquad 0\le q_a\le d_a,\qquad
 \bm{h}=-B(\bm{L},\bm{0}),
\end{align*}
where $d_t=U_t-L_t\le a_t^++a_t^-\le n$ and $d_e=1$.
In particular, $D\coloneqq\sum_a d_a\le mn+n$.
Thus \cref{cor:bounded-integer-flows}, with $w_a\equiv1$ and $R=1$,
gives the required approximation using polynomially many arithmetic
operations in $m+n$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}$.

Finally, if $Q=\{\bm{x}:A\bm{x}\le\bm{b}\}$ is a polytope with
only binary vertices, then $Q\subseteq[0,1]^n$, since a polytope is
the convex hull of its vertices. Adding the cube bounds therefore
does not change $Q$. The lower bounds
$\ell_t=-a_t^-$ hold throughout the cube, so taking these bounds
and $\bm{u}=\bm{b}$ puts $Q$ in the form of $P$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For the fixed graph $G$ and any matroid ${\mathcal{N}}$ on its edge
set $E$, given by an independence oracle, we approximate
\[
 Z_0\coloneqq
 \sum_{\substack{S\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{N}}):\\\deg_S(v)\le b_v\ \forall v}}\bm{w}^S.
\]
For rainbow matchings, take $b_v=1$ and let ${\mathcal{N}}$ be the partition
matroid allowing at most one edge of each color. For forests, take
the graphic matroid.
We first replace $Z_0$ by a weighted sum $Z_q$ that gives
a small weight to dependent sets, and bound the resulting error.
We then express $Z_q$ through a convolution coefficient and apply
\cref{thm:curvature-convolution}.

Delete zero-weight edges and edges incident to a vertex
$v$ with $b_v=0$, restricting ${\mathcal{N}}$ accordingly. Write $n\coloneqq|E|$; the case
$n=0$ has $Z_0=1$. Define the measure
\[
 \mu(S)\coloneqq
       \mathbf{1}[\deg_S(v)\le b_v\ \forall v]\bm{w}^S.
\]
Its support is downward closed.

For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, put $q\coloneqq\varepsilon/(8n)$ and define
\[
 Z_q\coloneqq\sum_{S\in\operatorname{supp}\mu}
                    \mu(S)q^{|S|-{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(S)}.
\]
Independent sets contribute exactly $Z_0$, since their exponent is
zero. To bound the additional contribution, for each $S\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$
choose a basis $I(S)$ of ${\mathcal{N}}|S$ by fixed-order greedy.
Then $I(S)\subseteq S$ satisfies the degree bounds,
$|S\setminus I(S)|=|S|-{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(S)$, and
$\mu(S)\le\mu(I(S))$ because $w_e\le1$.
The map $S\mapsto(I(S),S\setminus I(S))$ is injective. Therefore
\[
 Z_0\le Z_q
 \le\sum_{\substack{I\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\cap{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{N}})}}
       \mu(I)\sum_{T\subseteq E\setminus I}q^{|T|}
 \le(1+q)^nZ_0\le(1+\varepsilon/4)Z_0,
\]
where $(1+q)^n\le e^{\varepsilon/8}\le1+\varepsilon/4$.
{Thus an estimate of $Z_q$ with relative error at most
$\varepsilon/2$ also estimates $Z_0$ with relative error at most $\varepsilon$.}

To approximate $Z_q$, define
\[
 \mu_q(S)\coloneqq q^{|S|}\mu(S),\qquad
 \nu_q(T)\coloneqq q^{|T|-{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}^*}}(T)}.
\]
For every $T\subseteq E$, the matroid dual-rank identity is
\[
 {\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}^*}}(T)=|T|+{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(E\setminus T)-{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(E).
\]
Taking $T=E\setminus S$ gives
$\nu_q(E\setminus S)=q^{{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(E)-{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(S)}$. Hence
\[
 [\bm{x}^E](g_{\mu_q}g_{\nu_q})
 =\sum_{S\subseteq E}\mu_q(S)\nu_q(E\setminus S)
 =q^{{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(E)}Z_q.
\]

We now verify the hypotheses of \cref{thm:curvature-convolution}.
First, $\mu$ has upward spectral curvature $-1$.
Fix $S\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$ and put
$W_S\coloneqq\{e\in E\setminus S:S+e\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\}$.
Let $B$ be the unsigned incidence matrix of $W_S$ on the
vertices $v$ with $b_v-\deg_S(v)=1$, where at most one further incident
edge can be added. Let $d_e$ be its column sums, and put
$D\coloneqq\operatorname{diag}(w_e)$ on these edges.
Two available edges cannot be added together precisely when they
share such a vertex. Since $G$ is simple, they
share at most one vertex. The principal submatrix indexed by $W_S$ is
\[
 (A_S^{\mu,-1})_{W_S\times W_S}
 =DB^{\mathsf T}BD+
   \operatorname{diag}_e\bigl(w_e-(d_e-1)w_e^2\bigr)
 \succeq0.
\]
Indeed, $d_e\le2$ and $w_e\le1$. Unavailable edges contribute zero
rows and columns. Also, every addition ratio of $\mu$ is at most one.

Consequently, $\mu_q$ has curvature $-q$, since
$A_S^{\mu_q,-q}=q^2A_S^{\mu,-1}$.
The measure $\nu_q$ has full support and curvature $q$. To see this, consider
the contraction ${\mathcal{N}}^*/T$: its loops have addition ratio $q$, and
its nonloops have addition ratio one. In $A_T^{\nu_q,q}$ the loop
rows vanish, each nonloop parallel class gives a block $(1-q)J$,
where $J$ is the all-ones matrix, and all other entries vanish.
Thus both supports are downward closed and their curvatures sum to
zero. Their addition ratios are at most $q$ and one, respectively,
so we may take $\gamma=q$ and $\chi=q^{-1}$ in
\cref{thm:curvature-convolution}.\footnote{To meet the theorem's
requirement that $\chi$ be polynomial in the ground-set size, add
$\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil$ dummy elements forbidden by $\mu$ and made
loops of ${\mathcal{N}}$. This leaves the target and the coefficient above
unchanged, and makes $\chi=8n/\varepsilon$ polynomial in the enlarged
ground-set size. The enlargement is polynomial in $n$ and
$\varepsilon^{-1}$.}

Degree checks and greedy rank queries evaluate both
measures using the dual-rank identity above.
Both are positive at the empty set, and
\[
 \log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu_q}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu_q})
 \le 2n\log(1/q)+\sum_{e\in E}\log(1/w_e).
\]
This bound and $\chi=8n/\varepsilon$ are polynomial in the input length
and $\varepsilon^{-1}$. Apply \cref{thm:curvature-convolution} with
relative error $\varepsilon/2$ and divide its coefficient estimate by
$q^{{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(E)}$. {This gives an estimate of $Z_q$ with
relative error at most $\varepsilon/2$, and hence an estimate of $Z_0$
with relative error at most $\varepsilon$.}

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\lambda>0$ and $0<t\le1$, define the weight functions
\[
 \pi(S)\coloneqq\lambda^{|S|}\mathbf{1}[S\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})],
 \qquad
 \nu(S)\coloneqq t^{|S|-\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}(S)}\mathbf{1}[S\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})].
\]
Their common support ${\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})$ is downward closed and connected,
and $\pi\odot\nu=\mu_{\lambda}^{(t)}$. We claim that $\pi$ has
upward $0$-spectral curvature and $\nu^*$ has upward
$1$-spectral curvature. Assuming these claims, \cref{thm:poincare}
with $\eta=0$ and $\kappa=1$ gives the desired inequality:
the dynamics has rate $\pi(S+u)/\pi(S)=\lambda$ for every feasible
addition, so its Dirichlet form is exactly
${\mathcal{E}}_{\lambda}^{(t)}(f,f)$ by reversibility. The case $t=0$
follows by continuity of the finite sums, and $\lambda=0$
gives a point mass at $\varnothing$, for which both sides vanish.
It remains to verify the two claims.

First, for $S\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})$, the feasible additions are the nonloops of
${\mathcal{M}}/S$. Two distinct feasible additions $u,v$ are called
\emph{parallel} in ${\mathcal{M}}/S$ if $S+u+v\notin{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})$.
Together with equality, this is an equivalence relation on the
nonloops of ${\mathcal{M}}/S$, partitioning them into equivalence classes.
Thus $A_S^{\pi,0}$ is a direct
sum of blocks $\lambda^2J$ on these classes and zero
rows for infeasible additions, where $J$ denotes an all-ones
matrix. Thus $A_S^{\pi,0}\succeq0$, proving the first claim.

Second, fix $S\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})$, so
${\mathcal{U}}\setminus S\in\operatorname{supp}\nu^*$, and put
${\mathcal{K}}\coloneqq({\mathcal{N}}|_S)^*$.
For every $T\subseteq S$, applying \cref{eq:matroid-dual-rank}
to the matroid ${\mathcal{N}}|_S$ on ground set $S$ gives
\[
 \mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{K}}}(T)
 =|T|+\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}|_S}(S\setminus T)-\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}|_S}(S)
 =|T|+\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}(S\setminus T)-\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}(S).
\]
Since $S\setminus T\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})$, the definitions yield
\begin{align*}
 \frac{\nu^*(({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)\cup T)}{\nu^*({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)}
 &=\frac{\nu(S\setminus T)}{\nu(S)}
 =\frac{t^{|S\setminus T|-\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}(S\setminus T)}}
        {t^{|S|-\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}(S)}}
 =t^{-|T|+\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}(S)-\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}(S\setminus T)}
 =t^{-\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{K}}}(T)}.
\end{align*}
Consequently, $A_{{\mathcal{U}}\setminus S}^{\nu^*,1}$ is a direct sum of blocks
$\frac{1-t}{t^2}J$ on the equivalence classes under parallelism
among the nonloops of ${\mathcal{K}}$,
with zero rows at its loops and outside $S$. Since $0 < t\leq 1$, these blocks are
positive semidefinite.
